title: Friday night missed calls: where restaurant orders go
seoTitle: Friday night missed calls for restaurants | ROAL
description: Friday night missed calls often turn into hang-ups, voicemail, or orders that never reach the kitchen. Here’s how to close those gaps.
question: Why do restaurant missed calls Friday night turn into lost orders, and what can I do about it?
answer: On Friday night, missed calls usually turn into lost pickup or delivery orders because callers hang up, leave voicemail, or call the next place that answers. The fix is to answer more calls live, forward busy calls to a phone host, and make sure every order gets a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.
summary: You’ll learn where Friday night missed calls go and how to keep more orders from slipping away.
intro:
Friday night missed calls usually do not become orders. They turn into hang-ups, voicemails, or callers trying the next restaurant down the street.

That hurts most on your busiest night, when every pickup order matters and the kitchen is already moving fast. The good news is you can set up a simple system so unanswered calls still get handled, even when your team is tied up.

sections.h2: Why Friday night missed calls usually turn into lost orders
sections.body:
Friday night is when your phone gets the most pressure. People are ordering takeout, checking wait times, asking about specials, or trying to place a last-minute pickup order. If nobody picks up, many callers do not wait around.

A missed call can go in a few directions:
- The caller hangs up and calls another restaurant.
- The caller leaves voicemail, but by the time you hear it, they have already ordered somewhere else.
- The caller calls back once or twice, gets a busy signal, and gives up.
- The caller decides not to order at all.

That is why the problem is not just the missed ring. It is the order that never reaches your kitchen. If you want to understand the business impact, use [the missed call cost calculator](/tools/missed-call-calculator) with your own average ticket and Friday volume. For a simple example, say your average pickup order is $28 and you miss 6 calls that would have ordered. That is $168 in possible sales, before you count repeat business or upsells. Plug in your own numbers, because every shop is different.

sections.h2: What happens to the order after no one answers?
sections.body:
When nobody picks up, the order usually disappears into one of three places: nowhere, voicemail, or a staff member’s memory. None of those are good for a Friday night rush.

Here is the practical path many orders take when the phone is busy:
1. Caller hears ringing for a while.
2. Caller hangs up, or the call rolls to voicemail.
3. Caller either tries again or calls another place.
4. If they leave a message, someone has to listen, write it down, and call back.
5. By then, the caller may already be gone.

A clear phone plan fixes this. One option is to forward unanswered or busy calls to [ROAL](/about), which can take pickup and delivery orders from your live menu, answer hours and menu questions, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It can also hand off allergy-sensitive questions, complaints, and manager requests to staff with a summary. That matters on Friday night, when the goal is not just answering the phone. The goal is getting the order into the right place fast.

sections.h2: How to set up call forwarding for busy nights
sections.body:
If your phone system allows it, forwarding is the fastest way to catch overflow calls. The exact code depends on your carrier or phone system, so always confirm with them and test with a call before a rush.

Common setups include:
- Some landlines and carriers use *72 to forward all calls and *73 to turn it off.
- On some GSM mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off.
- **61*number# often forwards unanswered calls.
- **67*number# often forwards busy calls.
- Verizon Wireless often uses *72 / *73, and *71 for busy or no-answer forwarding.
- Business VoIP systems usually set forwarding in the web portal.

A simple Friday-night setup might be:
1. Keep your main line ringing in-house first.
2. Forward only unanswered or busy calls to the overflow line.
3. Test it before service with one real call.
4. Make sure the person or phone host on the other end knows your hours, address, and menu.

If you want a quick reference, use [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes). The important part is not the code itself. It is making sure a caller has somewhere to go when your team is in the weeds.

sections.h2: What a phone host should say on a Friday night
sections.body:
When the phone is ringing hard, the script should be short, clear, and built around your menu. The caller needs to know they reached the right place and that someone can help right away.

A useful opening line is: "Thanks for calling [restaurant name]. I can help with pickup or delivery orders, hours, and menu questions."

Then keep it moving with a simple order flow:
- Ask for the order first.
- Confirm sizes, modifiers, and notes.
- Ask for the caller’s name and phone.
- Give a ready time.
- Repeat the order back once.

For example, if a caller says, "Can I get two pepperoni pies, one well done, and a side of garlic knots?" the phone host should confirm the items, note the cooking preference, collect the name, and send the ticket to the kitchen screen.

ROAL does that from the restaurant’s live menu and also skips items marked sold out. It does not take card numbers over the phone, so payment stays with your normal process at pickup or delivery. That keeps Friday night simple for the caller and for your staff.

sections.h2: How much does one missed Friday order really cost?
sections.body:
You do not need a perfect model to see the problem. A rough example is enough to show why Friday night missed calls matter.

Use this table and swap in your own numbers:

| Example item | Your number |
|---|---:|
| Average order value | $28 |
| Missed calls that would have ordered | 6 |
| Possible sales lost | $168 |
| Delivery app commission on $168 if routed there at 20% | $33.60 |

sections.h2: A simple Friday-night playbook for your team
sections.body:
The cleanest fix is not one trick. It is a small playbook everyone can follow when the phone starts stacking up.

Try this:
1. Decide which calls must be answered live and which can roll to overflow.
2. Put your hours, address, parking note, and top menu questions in one place.
3. Train one line for staff: "If I cannot grab it, the overflow line handles pickup orders and questions."
4. Decide who checks the inbox for questions the host could not answer.
5. Review call history after service so you can spot repeated issues.

A practical example: if Friday night brings a dinner rush, your team can stay on the line for in-house customers while overflow calls go to an AI phone host. ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically once the owner claims the host, and the owner forwards the restaurant’s existing number to it. Forwarding can be turned off any time.

If you want more detail on the setup, the [How it works](/how-it-works) page shows how the restaurant website, Google Maps link, or menu upload becomes a working phone host in about a minute. That is useful for owners who do not want a big setup project before the weekend.

sections.h2: What to review after the rush ends
sections.body:
Friday night does not end when the last call stops ringing. The next step is checking what the phone taught you.

Look at three things in your dashboard or call log:
- Which calls were answered.
- Which questions came up again and again.
- Which orders needed staff help, like allergy questions or manager requests.

That review helps you tighten the next shift. For example, if callers keep asking about parking, add a short FAQ answer. If they keep asking about a sold-out item, update the menu editor right away. If the phone host could not answer a specific question, the owner can answer it once and the host knows it from then on.

ROAL includes call history with transcripts and recordings, a menu editor, hours, FAQs, upsell suggestions, and multi-location menus. That is useful after a Friday rush because you can see where calls slowed down and where callers needed more clarity.

If you want to try it with your own menu and hours, [build a free test host](/try). You can paste your restaurant website, Google Maps link, or "Name, City," test-call it in the browser, and decide from there.

faq.q: Where do missed calls go on Friday night at a restaurant?
faq.a: They usually go to hang-up, voicemail, or a callback that comes too late. On a busy Friday, many callers will not wait long if nobody answers. That means the order often ends up at another restaurant instead.

faq.q: Should I forward all calls or only busy and unanswered calls?
faq.a: That depends on how your shop runs. Many owners keep the main line active and forward only busy or unanswered calls during rush periods. Always confirm the forwarding code with your carrier or phone system and test with a real call before service.
